tagline: A sepoy of the East India Company's Bengal Army.
context: Indian soldiers formed the great majority of the Company's armies in 1857 — the Bengal Army alone contained tens of thousands of Indian sepoys. These were professional soldiers with oaths, pay, honours and families, drawn heavily from the high-caste communities of the Gangetic plain. From late 1856, grievances over overseas service, promotion, and the greased Enfield cartridge eroded their trust in their officers.
concerns: Religious and caste obligations — what the new cartridge meant for ritual purity
Pay, promotion and the changing terms of service
The oath of loyalty sworn to the Company versus trust eroding day by day
Family and village — what an uprising would cost those left behind

tagline: A cultivator in the villages of the Gangetic plain.
context: Most people in the region under upheaval in 1857 were cultivators. Rural life in the Gangetic plain was shaped by the land revenue that the Company demanded, by debts to moneylenders, by the monsoon, and by the authority of zamindars and officials. When armies marched, it was the villages that paid — in grain, animals, labour and safety.
concerns: The harvest and the monsoon — whether the family would eat
Land revenue — who would collect it, and what they would take
Which army's demands to obey when two sides both wanted supplies
Keeping family and home intact while the region slipped into conflict

tagline: A weaver, craftsman or workshop worker in a town of the Doab.
context: Nineteenth-century changes in trade pressed hard on artisans. Indian textiles and crafts faced competition from factory goods and shifts in colonial markets, and entire trades that depended on courts and armies struggled. During the upheaval of 1857, workshops closed, patrons vanished, soldiers commandeered materials, and the lines between self-preservation and alliance blurred.
concerns: The link between livelihoods, looms and books
Whether to keep working for whoever held the town
Protecting the tools and household of the trade
Trade and markets that had already been reshaped before 1857

tagline: A trader moving goods along roads that armies now contested.
context: Merchant communities financed trade, kept the Company's economy moving, and passed news along the roads they travelled. In 1857, the same roads carried soldiers, and the same warehouses were requisitioned by whatever authority held the district. Merchants had to weigh cargo against risk, and client against cause.
concerns: Security of goods, bullion and debt-notes
Which authority would honour contracts after the fighting
The interruption of supply routes and rising prices
Family capital — how much to risk on a road that armies controlled

tagline: A young learner in the world of books, schools and the city.
context: Cities like Delhi were centres of learning — Persian, Urdu, Arabic and newly English schools, printers, and teachers. Young people studying in 1857 were inheriting both an older world of letters and a newer colonial education. In the upheaval, institutions scattered and libraries were touched by the war; learning was itself interrupted.
concerns: Continuing study while war closed schools and scattered teachers
The new schools versus the older traditions of learning
Being asked to take sides in a conflict no book explained
What 'the youth' of a city were expected to be, and to become

tagline: A prince, noble or local authority inside a system of alliances.
context: India in 1857 was a patchwork of Company territory and princely states of every size. The Company's annexations — under the doctrine of lapse at Jhansi and Satara, and the takeover of Awadh in 1856 — alarmed rulers across India. Yet most major princes stayed loyal to the Company when the rebellion broke; those dispossessed, and many lesser authorities, faced a far harder choice.
concerns: Court, titles, income and the protection of a dynasty
Treaties with the Company versus appeals from the rebel proclamations
Which army to follow if two sides both asked for help
Subjects — landlords, peasants and soldiers — whose choices would outlive any court decree
